title: State Of The Raptors: It's Time To Learn Something New
text:
State Of The Raptors: It's Time To Learn Something New
Safe to say everyone is itching to see this team add size in the frontcourt
Neemias Queta was having his way with the Toronto Raptors. So was Luka Garza. Ditto, rookie Hugo Gonzalez.
One night later, Toronto looked ready to take the excuse that their flight to Brooklyn was delayed due to a mechanical issue and led to a 5 a.m. arrival. Maybe that would hold water against a legitimate playoff team, not so much against one that was 7-19 on the season entering Sunday night’s contest.
Tuesday night in Miami started to raise some red flags but Scottie Barnes led with physicality and the Raptors were able to increasingly take control before winning in blowout fashion with Masai Ujiri in attendance. Brandon Ingram being able to rest for the entire fourth quarter was a huge bonus. It’s just too bad Toronto doesn’t face Miami again until April.
Zooming out a bit further, Toronto is 3-2 since their NBA Cup exit. Do you take the positives of the wins in Miami twice and Milwaukee or drown in the sorrows of getting manhandled against Boston and Brooklyn? Realistically, you’ve got to balance the two.
The online commentary has ranged from calling the Raptors soft to a team lacking an identity. There is a palpable angst across the fan base, from needing to see this team add a seven-footer to a general need to ramp up the toughness to head coach Darko Rajakovic and the front office not being good enough.
Well, let’s dive into all aspects of the angst in making the fairest, most accurate judgment on the state of the Raptors at this current juncture.
Are The Raptors Soft?
Hugo Gonzalez storming down the lane and releasing a primal roar after a two-handed slam doesn’t make the Raptors soft the same way Ja’Kobe Walter puffing his chest to punctuate a run doesn’t make the opponents in those scenarios soft.
It was frustrating to watch these last two games, for sure, but the Raptors have shown real toughness in several wins this season — even as recently as in Miami last week where Scottie Barnes took over down the stretch. Boston had played Miami the night before the Raptors and won the game largely on shooting the lights out (21-for-43 on threes), turning a three-point game entering the fourth quarter into a 13-point victory.
Miami, a team Toronto had matched on the glass, grabbed 17 offensive rebounds against Boston primarily due to Bam Adebayo and Kel’el Ware. Still, when presented the opportunity, Gonzalez was able to make a play like this:
In a vacuum, that looks pretty familiar, doesn’t it?
If you’re wondering, Luka Garza — who grabbed nine(!) offensive rebounds against the Raptors — didn’t feature against the Heat and that may have been a lesson learned for Mazzulla heading into Toronto.
The s-word that is most relevant here is size, the Raptors have a lack of size problem. When Poeltl was available and playing well against the Heat, he could combine with Barnes to do what they usually do. Collin Murray-Boyles and Sandro Mamukelashvili both had good impacts off the bench. Just as much as Poeltl’s absence hurts in coping with big men, it gets exacerbated by the fact that the Raptors then get exposed for their lack of size at other positions as well.
Every bench player save for Murray-Boyles feels undersized for their position. Shead, Agbaji, Walter, and Dick each have their own strengths but aren’t going to magically add height and strength overnight to address the issue. Garza often got himself matched up against Shead or even Dick and they couldn’t handle his 6-foot-10, 240 pound frame at all.
Yes, the Nets also outrebounded the Raptors but that was largely due to Toronto’s offensive woes. The Raptors had more offensive boards while the Nets had 10 more defensive boards because of how many misses they had to collect.
This is why Barnes’ aggression level is such a key barometer for success. As we saw against the Heat, when he’s able to bring that level of intensity and energy and direct it towards attacking the basket it changes a whole lot. There should be others who can alleviate the pressure on him to do it every night but there aren’t, especially in the absence of Barrett and Poeltl. Barnes has had an excellent season and a two-game blip doesn’t make him soft, either.
What Does A Backup Big Man Change?
The most realistic path to improving the centre depth is with Ochai Agbaji’s $6.4 million contract and perhaps another salary filler depending on who is being acquired.
Phoenix’s Nick Richards has been in recent reports while Brooklyn’s Day’Ron Sharpe may be of interest as well. It’s hard to see the Clippers turning around their season with Ivica Zubac now out several weeks so Brook Lopez is an option I think is worth considering, too. At the same time, the Clippers may not feel comfortable letting go of Lopez when the centre depth is down their best option. Kevon Looney in New Orleans is another I’d be knocking on the door for to determine the asking price.
Richards would represent an improvement on the current situation but I’d still rather have any of the other three. I think both Lopez and Looney would offer more in terms of experience and helping build out the Raptors’ identity as well.
As much as it would ease the sense of dread every time it’s announced that Poeltl won’t play, it would also help alleviate the burden on Barnes having to protect the interior almost single-handedly (kudos to Murray-Boyles’ efforts in this regard). Accept that Poeltl’s back problems aren’t going away any time soon. These issues first surfaced in the second half of last season, a whole off-season clearly didn’t change much, and it has been a ticking time bomb since training camp and pre-season. For those who’ve been following along here for a while, I noted the concern back then.
A backup centre doesn’t dramatically alter the ceiling but it would help stabilize the floor when Poeltl is missing. Let’s not lose sight of how Quickley’s play has fluctuated depending on the availability of the big man, either. Home court advantage in the first round of the playoffs is there for the taking, don’t let perfect be the enemy of good here.
Do The Raptors Have An Identity?
Several have noted how the Celtics have an established identity and that, regardless of who plays, there is a consistency to their playing style and effort and the Raptors appear a long way from that.
Let’s remember that Joe Mazzulla has been a member of the Celtics franchise since 2019 when he first joined as an assistant coach. Both Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum have been with the franchise for even longer. Derrick White is a proven veteran and NBA champion. How many teams that have never made the playoffs with their current core have the Celtics’ level of clarity in identity?
We’re comparing apples and oranges here.
Bobby Webster spoke to the team before the season and made it clear his two expectations are that the team play smart and play hard. Rajakovic wants the team to have a defence-first mentality, they rank fourth in defensive efficiency on the season and have still been sixth over the last couple weeks. You’re not soft or completely lacking in identity if you can excel on that end of the floor consistently.
The offence needs to be better, help is needed to rebound better, and they understandably don’t have a championship or playoff-level DNA yet. Let’s not get carried away beyond that.
An identity will be defined by what they do for the majority of 82 games, not what they do in one or two of 82.
How Much Of The Blame Does Rajakovic Shoulder?
This is an important part of the calculus in Rajakovic’s first season with real expectations as well. The starting point in answering this is probably based on where you put the team’s accomplishments when the picture was much rosier.
Bad coaches extract less than what a team is capable of, good coaches extract what a team is reasonably capable of, great coaches extract everything and more out of what a team is capable of.
The Raptors having a top-5 offence until the Barrett injury was not on my bingo card for this season. If you are in the same boat as me, you have to give credit where its due and acknowledge that Rajakovic’s offensive philosophy coupled with what has generally been very good execution out of timeouts made the whole greater than the sum of its parts.
It is in the absence of Barrett that this is no longer the case. What we are seeing is that Rajakovic and the team have a great fastball but little else. Great teams are like Swiss Army knives and can adapt to the need of the hour. The Raptors are a good team that can be very good when firing on all cylinders but the floor can be considerably lower when any of the starters are missing.
Is there more meat to the bone in the absence of Barrett? My instincts tell me yes and so this stretch of offensive ineptitude has been disappointing. This team should not have dropped from fifth in offensive efficiency at 121.0 points per-100 possessions to dead-last at 108.4. Even staying out of the bottom-five would have been enough to collect a few of those wins that slipped away.
There are clear holes in the roster but he should have extracted more without Barrett. In particular, watching the complete lack of solutions when the Celtics and Nets turned to a zone defence has been rather discouraging. Rajakovic and the coaching staff, like the players, have had time since the NBA Cup defeat to make life a bit easier for the team.
I think Rajakovic is a good coach at this point in his career and is building a healthy culture. I think head coaches get the least leeway in their development potential and that just seems to be the reality of professional sports. For where the Raptors have been the last couple seasons and where they are now, he’s a good fit.
What About Webster?
Everything we’ve seen through the first 31 games shows us that this is a good team that is worth helping. At the very least, a move at the margins to improve the size and physicality of this team is a must.
Having all of Agbaji, Walter, Dick and Battle behind Barrett is too many. Agbaji having the opportunity to start the last several games has also been a good way to showcase him to opposing teams.
I understand that in-season trades are complicated. The front office has to be mindful of a potential “big fish” becoming available and preserving all assets for that possibility. Other teams are doing the same. The Raptors also lack trade salary flexibility as there are starters making a lot of money and then bench players making significantly less. The reality is that it’s likely a waiting game in the trade market and if you try too hard this early you could look desperate and have to fork over more than may be necessary come February.
In the meantime, bringing in help via a 10-day contract is important. The Raptors are 12-5 against sub-.500 teams and you don’t want to lose more of those games than you should. That record is also slightly skewed because the Hawks dropped under .500 last night (Raptors are 2-0 against the Hawks) and I would be surprised if they finished the season that way.
You can sign a player to a maximum of two 10-day contracts after which he must be signed for the remainder of the season. These 10-day contracts have a duration of 10 days or three games, whichever is longer. It may be a case of timing for the 20 days or the six games they want this centre to be available for.
There has also been a sense of frustration and a narrative that the Raptors haven’t cared about the centre position for several years. That was true during Vision 6’9 but I don’t think has held up as much since they awakened to the need for a big with the Poeltl trade. Let’s not forget that Christian Koloko was drafted and Ulrich Chomche was brought into the system as well. They couldn’t have predicted health issues for both forcing the organization to release them. They couldn’t have foreseen Jontay Porter getting involved in a betting scandal, either.
Could the position have been prioritized in the draft ahead of the franchise’s general philosophy of “best player available”? Yes, that was my stance prior to the draft. Still, you can’t deny the impact Murray-Boyles has been able to have and the encouragement that’s felt in his potential. It certainly is far from a bad pick.
TL;DR
To summarize, this is a team with a starting five that is more ready to win than its still young and developing bench. The absence of any one of the starters exposes that gap. They could certainly use a veteran presence, especially one that’s a big man.
It’s great that this team has proven itself worthy of being helped. Finishing in the top six with a 45-plus win season was always going to be considered a successful season. They’ve shown potential for a bit more and so the front office should look to make that happen as long as it helps both short and long-term.
I would encourage fans to find the joy in winning 45 or so games again. Don’t be the spoiled brat that thinks it’s only championship or bust. That doesn’t mean you’re settling or satisfied, but rather just embracing the journey to the top. Rome wasn’t built in a day, I’m told. I’ve received several messages on social media saying this is destined to be nothing more than a “meh” or “mediocre” season.
Personally, this is a new cycle and it’d be great to witness this group experience the playoffs — even better with home court advantage — and then you use all of the lessons to keep building from there.
Here’s wishing you and yours a happy holiday season! Thank you so much to those of you who subscribe, and if you haven’t hit that subscribe button yet, what better time than with RJ Barrett nearing a return and trade season approaching!
